analysis.one_liner: Removes the legal shield that protects ICE agents from being sued for violating people's rights.
analysis.headline: Introduced Aug. 8, 2025 with 2 cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agents can usually avoid paying damages when they violate someone's constitutional rights, under a court-made doctrine called qualified immunity: unless the right was 'clearly established' in earlier court cases, and unless the agent acted unreasonably, the case is dismissed. This bill would abolish both parts of that shield for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents. Anyone harmed by an ICE agent could then take the agent to court and recover damages even if the law wasn't clearly settled beforehand.
analysis.who_benefits: People detained, searched, or injured by ICE agents who would otherwise have no way to recover money damages. It would also give ICE agents a stronger personal incentive to follow the Constitution, since they could personally be held liable for violations.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends 42 U.S.C. 1983, the federal law that lets people sue government officials for violating their constitutional rights, to bar ICE agents from using the two standard qualified immunity defenses: that they acted in good faith, or that the violated right was not 'clearly established' at the time.
It applies to suits brought under section 1983 'or any other Federal law' against a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
The bill's stated purpose is to end qualified immunity specifically for ICE agents.

analysis.who_pays: ICE agents facing lawsuits, and indirectly the federal government, which typically indemnifies (pays judgments for) its agents. Immigration enforcement operations could also face more litigation and slower action.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: removing the good-faith defense means agents can be made to pay for conduct they reasonably believed was lawful at the time, which critics argue will chill energetic enforcement and drive good people out of the job.
More 1983 litigation against agents means more defense costs, and judgments are commonly paid by the government rather than the individual agent, so taxpayers may absorb much of the cost.
The bill is narrow by design: it strips immunity only from ICE agents, not from other federal or local law enforcement, leaving the same doctrine intact elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people subject to ICE operations, the benefit is real: a working path to damages when agents violate their rights, instead of cases being thrown out on immunity grounds. The cost is more litigation and a harder environment for enforcement agents. The bill is also deliberately narrow, so it does not resolve the broader qualified immunity debate; it picks one agency, one that has been at the center of many recent enforcement controversies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-MI) introduced the bill on August 8, 2025, joined by Rep. Jan Schakowsky as an original cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill has 2 cosponsors, both Democrats.
No further action — no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, ICE agents keep their current qualified immunity shield, and no one has been made newly accountable. With the Congress still in session, the outcome is not final.

for.name: Rep. Shri Thanedar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has only Democratic support — a Democratic sponsor and 2 Democratic cosponsors, none from the Republican majority — and no Republican has acted on it.

industries.industry: Federal immigration enforcement (ICE agents and the agency's operations)
industries.note: The bill strips ICE agents of qualified immunity, exposing them personally to damages lawsuits for constitutional violations. ICE's interest in keeping that shield runs against the people it detains and searches, who currently often cannot recover for violations.

analysis.trajectory: With 2 cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action a month after referral, the realistic path is that the bill stays in the House Judiciary Committee and dies at the end of this Congress without a hearing or vote, like most non-controversial-to-the-majority single-sponsor immigration bills.
